title: What Is On-Premise iPaaS and How Does It Work in 2026?
summary: On-premise iPaaS allows organizations to manage data workflows within private infrastructure. You can evaluate if local hosting meets your security needs.
body_markdown:
## How private integration engines process data behind firewalls


Private integration engines ensure data sovereignty by isolating the execution of your automated workflows within your corporate network while keeping administrative management in a secure, centralized interface.


This architecture prevents raw data payloads from traversing the public internet, satisfying the primary requirement of your internal risk committees who forbid the transmission of PII to third-party cloud environments.


### Control plane vs runtime plane in on-premise iPaaS


The separation of the control plane from the runtime plane allows you to manage integrations through a unified dashboard while keeping the actual data processing strictly local.


In this model, the Control Plane is the design and monitoring hub where you build logic and view metadata.


The Runtime Plane is the execution engine that interacts with your internal databases and applications.


The 'Control Plane' (UI/Management) sits in a cloud or management zone and the 'Runtime Plane' (Execution Engine) sits behind your corporate firewall, with data remaining local.


### How data and commands flow between planes


The visual logic of this architecture relies on a strict unidirectional flow for sensitive information.


The Control Plane sends execution commands and logic updates down to the Runtime Plane, but the Runtime Plane only sends back metadata, such as success or failure logs, without including the actual data payloads.


This ensures that the cloud-based management layer never sees the contents of your internal ERP or database. By visualizing the boundary, you can see that the Execution Agent acts as a one-way gatekeeper that processes data locally and reports status only.


### Logic mapping without data exposure


When a user builds a workflow in the cloud-hosted Control Plane, they must map data fields between steps. To prevent PII from leaking to the UI during this design phase, the system uses sample schemas rather than live production data.


The local Runtime Plane generates a structural template of the data it sees behind the firewall and sends only this non-sensitive schema up to the designer.


The user sees a field named "Customer_Email" in the UI, but the actual email address "[\[email protected\]](https://www.activepieces.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#0b7e786e794b6e736a667b676e25686466) " never leaves the local agent.


### Achieving total isolation with air-gapped hosting


For organizations requiring absolute data sovereignty, the hybrid model is insufficient because the control plane remains external. A true on-premise deployment involves self-hosting both the control plane and the runtime plane within your own private infrastructure.


By hosting the UI and the metadata database locally, you eliminate the need for any outbound connection to a vendor's dashboard. This configuration is essential for air-gapped environments where systems must operate without internet access to prevent external surveillance or data exfiltration.


A stripped self-hosted build is how most vendors monetise this control, but Activepieces aims to provide the same SSO, SCIM, custom RBAC, audit logs, and secret manager integration in its air-gapped Enterprise build as it does in the managed cloud.


Regulated organisations like MoneyGram and FundingSocieties run this edition in production to maintain governance without sacrificing the feature set.


You can verify this by comparing the enterprise feature list in the self-hosted air-gapped documentation against the managed cloud tier pinned to a SOC 2 Type II region.


You can update a workflow using Claude Opus 5.5 for complex logic design in the cloud UI, but the actual execution against a local SQL Server happens entirely behind your firewall.


### Secure connectivity via site-to-site VPNs


Establishing a secure tunnel between the management layer and the local runtime is the only way to maintain centralized oversight without exposing your internal execution engine to the open web. A Site-to-Site VPN or a dedicated TLS-encrypted gateway typically achieves this.


These tools ensure that only authenticated traffic from the control plane can trigger local actions. By restricting ingress to a single, hardened point of entry, your IT security team can apply granular firewall rules that prevent unauthorized external actors from reaching your integration environment.


### Managing local execution agents


Local execution agents are containerized services that reside on your internal hardware to act as the hands and feet of your integration platform.


These agents facilitate direct connections to sensitive internal resources, such as Active Directory, providing the necessary identity context for your automated onboarding workflows.


Every credential Activepieces touches, from API keys to OAuth tokens, can be routed to your own secret manager instead of a vendor database in both the self-hosted and enterprise cloud tiers.


By configuring a self-hosted instance against an external secret manager, you ensure that no vendor holds the credentials your business runs on.


This allows teams to inspect the database and confirm that sensitive secrets are not stored within the iPaaS itself, a capability missing from cloud-only providers like Zapier or Make.


They also connect to on-premise ERP systems, allowing for the synchronization of financial records without cloud exposure. Private LLM instances, such as Mistral Large 4 running on your local GPUs, ensure that proprietary prompts never leave your air-gapped environment.


Because these agents are managed as standard Docker containers or Kubernetes pods, your infrastructure team can apply existing patching schedules and resource limits. This ensures your integration layer adheres to the same stability standards as any other tier-one application.
